extracted.intended_audience: international patent examiners and applicants (PCT applicants, receiving Offices, International Authorities)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and examining PCT patent claims (clarity, support, conciseness, interpretation, product/process claims) and for claiming/establishing priority dates under the PCT. Addresses examiner practices, examples, and procedural steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of claims (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim complies with clarity if a person skilled in the art can determine the boundaries of the claimed invention with a reasonable degree of certainty; breadth is not automatically lack of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the scope of the subject matter embraced by the claims is clear and the applicant has not indicated a different intended scope, the claims are clear. Independent claims should specify all essential features except those implied by generic terms (e.g., 'bicycle' need not mention wheels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claim must specify essential features
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention except insofar as such features are implied by generic terms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For process claims producing a product, the claimed process should, when carried out reasonably by a skilled person, necessarily have as its end result that particular product; otherwise internal inconsistency/lack of clarity arises. For product claims where invention modifies a well-known product, it is sufficient to identify the product and specify what is modified and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of relative and degree terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative or vague terms (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong') should not be used unless they have a well-recognized meaning in the art or are defined in the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term of degree appears, the examiner should determine whether a skilled person would understand its meaning from a standard for measuring that degree in the description or from the prior/state of the art. Examiner may invite applicant to define or excise such terms, provided amendment does not add subject matter. An applicant cannot rely on an unclear term to distinguish from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims defining by result to be achieved (result-type claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that attempt to define an invention or feature by a result to be achieved should generally be objected to for lack of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No objection if the invention can only be defined that way and the result is achievable without undue experimentation, e.g., verified by tests or procedures adequately specified in the description and involving nothing more than routine trial and error. Example: ashtray defined by a resulting automatic extinguishing effect is acceptable if description enables routine tests to determine dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of products by parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: A product may be defined solely by its parameters where other definitions are inadequate, provided the parameters can be clearly and reliably determined by the description or objective procedures recognized in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same applies to process features defined by parameters. Use of non-art-recognized parameters or inaccessible measuring apparatus may be objectionable. Beware of attempts to disguise lack of novelty by employing unusual parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims referencing features of use or a second product
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining an apparatus/product by reference to the use relationship to a second product (not part of the claim) can cause lack of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims must either clearly define the individual product (e.g., 'connectable' instead of 'connected') or be directed to a combination (e.g., 'engine comprising a cylinder head'). It may be permissible to define dimensions of first product by general reference to the shape/dimensions of a second related product where reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of approximating terms ('about', 'approximately')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'about' or 'approximately' require careful examination to determine whether their meaning is sufficiently clear in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should judge if such words prevent unambiguous distinction from prior art; if they do, raise objection for lack of novelty or inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of trademarks and similar expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks characterize commercial origin rather than technical properties; they should generally be removed from claims unless unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may be allowed exceptionally if generally recognized as having a precise meaning. Examiner should invite removal where trademarks introduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting effect of expressions of preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions such as 'preferably', 'for example', 'such as', 'more particularly' should be treated as non-limiting and not to restrict claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features following such expressions should be regarded as optional and not limit the claim unless otherwise clearly stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may include disclaimers or negative limitations to exclude subject matter, and negative language is not per se ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative limitations render a claim unclear if they attempt to claim by excluding what applicant did not invent rather than clearly reciting what was invented. If alternatives are positively recited in the description they may be explicitly excluded in claims. The mere absence of positive recitation is not a basis for exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness of claims (entirety and individual claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be concise both as a set and individually; undue repetition or an undue multiplicity of trivial claims may fail the conciseness requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undue multiplicity or duplicative claims that confuse rather than clarify may be objected to. Individual claims containing long recitations or unimportant details making scope indefinite may be objectionable. See Appendix for divergent authority practices on conciseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support in description (Article 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims shall be fully supported by the description; there must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the scope must not be broader than justified by description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general rule, claims are supported unless there are well-founded reasons to believe a skilled person could not extend the teaching to the whole claimed field using routine methods. Vague assertions with no technical content provide no basis. When raising lack-of-support, reasons should, where possible, be supported by a published document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and complete disclosure / sufficiency (Article 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure must be sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art as of the international filing date without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable amount of trial and error is permissible; the person skilled in the art may use general knowledge to supplement the disclosure. Particularly in unexplored technologies, undue experimentation standard applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when determining whether undue experimentation is needed: breadth of claims; nature of invention; general knowledge of skilled person; level of predictability in the art; amount of direction provided in the application (including examples and references); and amount of experimentation required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breadth of claims is relevant because skilled person must be able to carry out entire scope. Representative examples plus explanation of how they apply to the whole claim are ordinarily sufficient. Consider also whether experimentation is routine or goes beyond routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency commensurate with the claims (generalisation limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible extent of generalization from particular examples depends on the prior art and whether it is reasonable to predict that all variants covered by the claims have the ascribed properties or uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate claim is not so broad as to go beyond the invention nor so narrow as to deprive applicant of a just reward. Obvious modifications and equivalents described should not be questioned. Examiner may invite applicant to establish that invention applies to whole claimed field or to restrict claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of claims to disclosure (consistency and missing essential elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be fully supported by description/drawings showing applicant claimed subject matter recognized and described on filing date; claims inconsistent with disclosure or missing essential elements fail the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If essential element for function/operation is missing from claim, it's not commensurate with description. Examples: functional property relying on an undisclosed additive; contradictions between claims and description. Claims covering speculative, unexplored possibilities may be objectionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim support and means equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may define a feature in terms of its function even where only one example is given if a skilled person would appreciate other means for same function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If description gives impression the function is to be carried out in a particular way with no hint of alternatives, a claim embracing other means may not comply with support. Mere vague statements that alternatives 'may' be adopted may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of chemical compounds by parameters (support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization solely by parameters may be appropriate when supported by relevant identifying characteristics showing applicant recognized and described the claimed invention at the time of filing (partial structure, properties, function/structure correlations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficient relevant identifying characteristics are required to evidence recognition of the invention on filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of sufficiency and support determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with sufficiency (Article 5) and support for claims (Article 6) are determined independently; a claim may fail one or both requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim too broad to be supported may also render disclosure insufficient to enable the whole claimed scope; both objections can apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims practices (divergent approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities have divergent practices: (1) dependent claim referring to more than one other claim should refer only alternatively; multiple dependent claims cannot form basis for other multiple dependent claims; or (2) dependent claim may refer alternatively or cumulatively and multiple dependent claims may form a basis for other multiple dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either alternative guideline may be relied upon by an International Authority as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of claims when description provides special definitions (divergent practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities diverge on whether special definitions in the description should be used for claim interpretation or whether the claim should be amended to make meaning clear from claim wording alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative practices: (1) use the description's special definition for interpreting the claim (do not limit claims to examples); take into account description, drawings and general knowledge if wording needs interpretation; or (2) require amendment so meaning is clear from claim alone and read claim attempting to make technical sense even departing from strict literal wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of 'use' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For international search/examination, a 'use' claim of the form 'use of substance X as an insecticide' may be regarded as equivalent to a process claim 'a process of killing insects using substance X.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a claim should not be interpreted as directed to the substance per se intended for insecticide use, nor to an apparatus in which it is used. Note that some designated/elected States may consider 'when/whenever used' claims improper process claims under national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims practices (divergent approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities have divergent practices regarding product-by-process claims: (1) construe as a claim to the product per se possessing characteristics derived from the manufacturing process; patentability does not depend on method of production (product not novel merely because made by new process), or (2) construe as relating to and anticipated only by a product actually produced by the recited process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either alternative guideline may be relied upon by an International Authority as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness divergent practice detail (A5.42[1] and [2])
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergent practices on conciseness: (1) claims may be objected to as unduly multiplied or duplicative when repetitious and confusing; (2) number of claims must be considered relative to nature/scope of invention; undue repetition or multiplicity of trivial claims rendering it burdensome may violate conciseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether number of claims is reasonable depends on facts/circumstances; presentation should not obscure protection sought. Number of alternatives within a single claim should not make it unduly burdensome to determine subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to priority and international filing date (Article 11 and related rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application is accorded the international filing date when it satisfies Article 11 requirements; an application may claim priority of an earlier application and in that case the priority date is used to calculate certain time limits and for international examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International filing date may remain the only effective date; priority date is important for written opinion and international preliminary examination report. Relevant dates for international search vs written opinion differ and are set out elsewhere in PCT guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for a valid claim to priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Several conditions: the earlier application must have been made by the applicant or predecessor in title; it must have been filed in/for a Paris Convention country or WTO member; and the international application must generally be filed within 12 months (priority period) of the earlier filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority claim is not void only because international filing date is later than expiry of priority period if within two additional months (Rule 26bis.2) to allow for restoration. Earlier application may be national, regional or international and may be for a patent, utility model or inventor's certificate. Other conditions in paragraphs 6.04 and 6.11-6.17 apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: First application and withdrawn/abandoned first application exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally the earlier application must be the first application filed for the invention, but a subsequent application can be considered the first for priority if the first was withdrawn/abandoned/refused without public inspection and without outstanding rights and had not served as a basis for claiming priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner will not normally examine this unless clear evidence exists of an earlier application, but may invite applicant to satisfy the examiner that no rights remained outstanding where priority is important due to intervening prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple priorities and allocation of priority dates
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application may claim priority from more than one earlier application even from different countries; each element of the application gets the priority date of the earliest priority application which discloses it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different embodiments A and B were disclosed in different earlier applications, each embodiment is accorded its respective priority date. A combination of features disclosed only separately in different priorities is not entitled to earlier priority and will have the international filing date unless an explicit reference allows combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: When examiner must consider validity of priority claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner need not investigate priority validity when preparing written opinion, except where subject matter relevant to novelty/inventive step was disclosed on or after claimed priority date and before international filing date or where prior art publications/applications fall under Rule 64.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the examiner must satisfy himself that the claimed priority date(s) may be accorded to the appropriate parts of the international application and may consider validity of priority dates of other applications/patents as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining entitlement to priority (specificity and disclosure test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled to the priority date, the subject matter of the claim must be explicitly or inherently disclosed in the priority document, including features implicit to a skilled person; the test is the same as for Article 34(2)(b) amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must be specific; mere broad or implied references are insufficient though exact correspondence is not required—there must be, in substance, disclosure of all important elements. Implicit disclosures (e.g., general concept of 'releasable fastening' disclosed by examples of nut-and-bolt, spring catch etc.) can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences if priority tests not satisfied
rubrics_metrics.description: If priority tests are not satisfied for a particular earlier application, the relevant date of the claim will be the priority date of the earliest application which does satisfy the tests, or otherwise the international filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should identify the earliest document providing required disclosure; lack of entitlement affects prior art assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical requirements for claiming priority (procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant wishing to claim priority must state this on the request (Form PCT/RO/101) giving particulars of the previous filing, though later corrections (addition/deletion) are permitted under Rule 26bis within time limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must, in addition to particulars, either (i) submit the priority document to the International Bureau or receiving Office within 16 months of the priority date (unless already filed with receiving Office), (ii) request receiving Office to prepare and transmit the document to the IB where priority document is issued by the receiving Office, or (iii) request the IB before international publication to obtain the priority document from a digital library if available in accordance with Administrative Instructions.
